title: Why does `LIMIT ... OFFSET` pagination get slower on deep pages (the DB scans and discards all preceding rows — O(n) per page), and how does keyset/cursor pagination (`WHERE id > :last_seen ORDER BY id LIMIT n`) stay O(log n) at any depth?
shortTitle: Why LIMIT/OFFSET pagination gets slower on deep pages, and keyset pagination
topicTitle: Why does `LIMIT ... OFFSET` pagination get slower on deep pages (the DB scans an

s1_definition.profdef: Offset-based pagination (`LIMIT n OFFSET m`) forces the database to read and discard all `m` preceding rows before returning the page, so cost grows linearly with page depth — O(m). Keyset (cursor) pagination replaces the offset with a `WHERE` condition on the last-seen sorted key (`WHERE id > :last_seen ORDER BY id LIMIT n`), letting an index seek jump directly to the start of the page, so cost stays O(log n) at any depth.
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh wants page five hundred of his transaction history. With OFFSET, the clerk counts past the first ten thousand transactions one by one and throws them away just to hand over the next ten — exhausting on deep pages. With keyset pagination, Rajesh says "continue from the last transaction I saw," and the clerk uses the index to jump straight there, which is just as fast on page five hundred as on page one.
s1_definition.oneliner: OFFSET re-reads everything before the page (slower the deeper you go); keyset seeks straight to the page using the last-seen key (fast at any depth).
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Offset-based pagination (`LIMIT n OFFSET m`) forces the database to read and discard all `m` preceding rows before returning the page, so cost grows linearly with page depth — O(m). Keyset (cursor) pagination replaces the offset with a `WHERE` condition on the last-seen sorted key (`WHERE id > :last_seen ORDER BY id LIMIT n`), letting an index seek jump directly to the start of the page, so cost stays O(log n) at any depth.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Rajesh wants page five hundred of his transaction history. With OFFSET, the clerk counts past the first ten thousand transactions one by one and throws them away just to hand over the next ten — exhausting on deep pages. With keyset pagination, Rajesh says "continue from the last transaction I saw," and the clerk uses the index to jump straight there, which is just as fast on page five hundred as on page one.

**One line to remember:** OFFSET re-reads everything before the page (slower the deeper you go); keyset seeks straight to the page using the last-seen key (fast at any depth).

sections.s2_technical:
With offset pagination, a query like `SELECT * FROM transactions ORDER BY txn_id LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10000` cannot magically start at row ten thousand. The database must produce the sorted stream, count through the first ten thousand rows, discard every one of them, and only then emit the next ten. The discarded work is pure waste, and it grows with the offset. Page one discards zero rows; page one thousand discards ten thousand rows every single time it is requested. That is why deep pages crawl — it is O(offset) work per page.

Keyset pagination removes the offset entirely. Instead of asking for "skip ten thousand," you remember the sort key of the last row shown — say the last `txn_id` was 10000 — and the next page is `SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE txn_id > 10000 ORDER BY txn_id LIMIT 10`. If `txn_id` is indexed, the database performs an index seek directly to the entry just after 10000 and reads ten rows. It never touches the preceding ten thousand. Because an index seek is a B-tree descent, the cost is O(log n) to locate the start plus O(n) to read the page, and crucially it is identical whether you are on page one or page one million.

The trade-off is that keyset pagination gives you "next page" and "previous page" navigation rather than arbitrary "jump to page 500." For infinite-scroll feeds, transaction histories, and APIs, that is exactly what you want. For a true random-access page picker you need a stable sort and a composite cursor.

The cursor must be on a unique, ordered column, or a composite of columns that together are unique, otherwise rows with equal keys can be skipped or duplicated across pages. A common pattern is ordering by a timestamp plus the primary key as a tiebreaker: `WHERE (created_at, id) > (:last_ts, :last_id) ORDER BY created_at, id LIMIT n`, which requires a composite index on `(created_at, id)`.

Keyset also plays well with stable results under concurrent inserts. With OFFSET, inserting rows while a user paginates shifts everything and causes duplicates or skips. With keyset, you are anchored to a real key, so new rows inserted after your cursor simply appear on later pages naturally.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — At the National Bank of India, Rajesh scrolls his years-long transaction history. The first few pages load instantly, but by the time he reaches older transactions the app stalls for seconds. This is exactly how OFFSET pagination behaves — each deep page re-reads and discards everything before it.

Problem 2 — While Rajesh scrolls, new transactions keep posting to his account. With OFFSET, the same transaction sometimes appears twice or a transaction is skipped as rows shift. This is exactly how OFFSET loses stability under concurrent inserts.

Problem 3 — We switch to "load more from where you left off." This is exactly how keyset pagination works — anchor on the last-seen key and seek forward.

We will build a `TransactionHistoryService` with both an offset method (to show the problem) and a keyset method using `(txnDate, txnId)` as the cursor, backed by a composite index, so deep pages stay fast.

##### 4b. SQL Database Script

```sql
-- V1__keyset_index.sql
-- Composite index matching the keyset order: (account_id, txn_date, txn_id)
-- Enables an index seek directly to the cursor position at any depth.
CREATE INDEX idx_hist_keyset ON transactions(account_id, txn_date, txn_id);

-- SLOW: deep offset re-reads and discards 10000 rows
-- SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE account_id='SAV2001'
--   ORDER BY txn_date, txn_id LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10000;   -- O(offset)

-- FAST: keyset seeks straight to the row after the cursor
-- SELECT * FROM transactions
--   WHERE account_id='SAV2001'
--     AND (txn_date, txn_id) > ('2024-03-01', 55123)
--   ORDER BY txn_date, txn_id LIMIT 10;                -- O(log n)
```

##### 4c. Configuration File

```yaml
# application.yml
spring:
  datasource:
    url: jdbc:postgresql://localhost:5432/bankdb
    username: bank_app
    password: ${DB_PASSWORD}
  jpa:
    show-sql: true
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build and run
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -jar target/history-service-1.0.0.jar

# Prove the difference with EXPLAIN ANALYZE
# OFFSET (watch rows removed by offset grow with depth):
psql bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE account_id='SAV2001' \
  ORDER BY txn_date, txn_id LIMIT 10 OFFSET 10000;"

# KEYSET (index seek, constant work at any depth):
psql bankdb -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM transactions WHERE account_id='SAV2001' \
  AND (txn_date, txn_id) > ('2024-03-01', 55123) ORDER BY txn_date, txn_id LIMIT 10;"
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh's `SAV2001` history, page size ten, requesting a deep page.

Step 1: First page. The client has no cursor, so the service calls `firstPage` with limit ten. The index seeks to the start of Rajesh's transactions and reads ten rows. The last row's `(txnDate, txnId)` becomes the cursor the client stores.

Step 2: Next page. The client sends back the cursor, say `('2024-03-01', 55123)`. The service calls `nextPage`. The query condition `(txn_date, txn_id) > ('2024-03-01', 55123)` lets the composite index seek directly to the row after the cursor.

Step 3: Deep page. Even on the five-hundredth page, the cursor still points to a real key, so the index seek jumps straight there and reads ten rows. No preceding rows are read or discarded. The work is identical to page two.

Step 4: Contrast with OFFSET. Had we used `OFFSET 10000`, the database would produce the sorted stream and discard ten thousand rows before returning ten — wasted work that grows with depth.

Step 5: Under concurrent inserts, new transactions post while Rajesh scrolls. Because keyset is anchored to a real key, those new rows naturally appear on later pages without duplicating or skipping anything.

```
2026-10-25 13:50:40 INFO  TransactionHistoryService - First page for SAV2001 (10 rows)
2026-10-25 13:50:41 INFO  TransactionHistoryService - Next page for SAV2001 after (2024-03-01, 55123) — seek, not scan
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Rajesh scrolls transaction history (page size 10)

  OFFSET pagination (gets slower with depth)
    page 1:  LIMIT 10 OFFSET 0      → read 10               O(1)
    page 100: LIMIT 10 OFFSET 990   → read+discard 990 +10  O(offset)
    page 1000: LIMIT 10 OFFSET 9990 → read+discard 9990 +10 O(offset)  ✗ slow

  KEYSET pagination (constant at any depth)
    page 1:  firstPage LIMIT 10                                   → index seek
    cursor = (2024-03-01, 55123)
    page N:  WHERE (txn_date,txn_id) > (2024-03-01,55123) LIMIT 10
             │ idx_hist_keyset seeks straight to row after cursor  O(log n)  ✓ fast
    ▼
  Same latency on page 1 and page 1,000,000
```

```
  └───────────────┬───────────────┘
                  │ uses
                  ▼
  ┌─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │   <<interface>> TransactionRepository    │
  │  + firstPage(acct, limit): List          │
  │  + nextPage(acct, lastDate, lastId, lim) │ ← (date,id) > cursor, index seek
  └─────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Contract for nextPage():
    Pre:  cursor = last row's (txnDate, txnId); composite index exists
    Post: returns up to `size` rows strictly after the cursor, sorted
    Perf: O(log n) seek regardless of page depth
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Offset pagination gets slower on deep pages because the database cannot magically start at row ten thousand. For LIMIT ten OFFSET ten thousand, it must produce the sorted stream, count through and discard all ten thousand preceding rows, and only then return the next ten. That discarded work is pure waste and it grows with the offset, so page one is instant but page one thousand crawls — it is order-of-offset work every time the page is requested. Offset also loses stability under concurrent inserts, because new rows shift the window and cause duplicates or skips.

Keyset, or cursor, pagination fixes this by removing the offset entirely. Instead of skipping rows, I remember the sort key of the last row shown and ask for everything after it: WHERE the sort key is greater than the last-seen key, ORDER BY that key, LIMIT n. If the sort key is indexed, the database performs an index seek directly to the row after the cursor and reads only the page. The cost is a B-tree descent plus the page read, which is order log n, and it is identical whether you are on page one or page one million.

The one requirement is that the cursor must be on a unique ordered column, or a composite of columns that are unique together, backed by a matching composite index. A very common banking pattern is ordering by a timestamp with the primary key as a tiebreaker, using a row-value comparison on the pair and a composite index on that pair. The trade-off is that keyset gives natural next-page and previous-page navigation rather than arbitrary jump-to-page-500, which is exactly right for transaction histories, feeds, and APIs.

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh's multi-year transaction history loaded instantly on the first pages but stalled for seconds once he scrolled deep, and transactions sometimes appeared twice because new ones kept posting while he scrolled. I replaced offset pagination with keyset pagination anchored on the transaction date and id pair, backed by a composite index on account, date, and id. Deep pages became as fast as the first page because the index seeks straight to the cursor, and the duplicates disappeared because the cursor is anchored to a real key. The sentence I always remember is that offset re-reads everything before the page while keyset seeks straight to it, so keyset stays fast at any depth.
